promise: Fixed upfront price · no hidden costs · lifetime labour warranty · same-day return

paths.name: Field Foundations
paths.who: Every Install and Service Tech, done first in weeks 1–2. (Sales Techs get the key rules in their refresh module, x1.)
paths.summary: The Proximity standard every tech works to: what we promise customers, how we stay safe, how we use ServiceTitan, how we treat customers (including when they complain), how we document, how we get paid, and how the three roles hand work to each other.

modules.title: The Proximity Standard & Our Promise
modules.objective: Know who we are, what we promise every customer, and why customers pay a premium for us.
modules.assessor: Lead tech in their trade (Service or Install); Charlotte (interim manager) as backup
lessons: Who we are: premium Sydney plumbing, 4.9★ from 2,500+ Google reviews
Who we serve: owner-occupiers, landlords and property managers, strata buildings
Our promise: fixed upfront price, no hidden costs, lifetime labour warranty, same-day return
Why we never charge by the hour (but every price is built on hours)
Where every dollar of a job goes, and why discounts hurt
Your truck is a business: the $200K-per-truck-per-month target
What's in it for you: pay, bonuses and growth
key_points: We never compete on price. Competitors like Mr Emergency compete on price and speed; we compete on trust and quality.
The promise is what customers pay for, and every tech must be able to explain it the same way. [CONFIRM: approved wording for the lifetime labour warranty and same-day return, including exclusions]
Customers get a fixed upfront price, so unestimated hours and unbilled materials come out of our profit, not the customer's pocket.

Where every dollar goes: about 50% labour and materials, 30% running the business, 20% profit (the 50% gross profit / 20% net profit guardrails). On a $1,000 job that's about $200 profit, so a 10% discount ($100) throws away half of it.
Our reputation is the 4.9★ review base. Every visit adds to it or damages it.
[CONFIRM] Whether to mention the 13th-month bonus (from Dec 2026) here as the payoff of a healthy business.
signoff: Can explain the promise (fixed price, lifetime labour warranty, same-day return) in their own words
Can explain why a 10% discount throws away half the profit
Van and uniform meet presentation standard on inspection
confirm: How much of the financial model techs should see

lessons: Site risk assessment and SWMS before you start
The right PPE on every job
Isolate water or gas before starting
Asbestos awareness in Sydney homes (fibro, AC pipe, old vinyl): stop and ask if unsure
Confined spaces, pits and roof work
Hot works and gas safety
Sewage, hygiene and PPE
Driving, fleet and fatigue
Licences: what you can do licensed vs supervised (apprentices and trainees)
Compliance paperwork and certificates lodged on time [VERIFY current NSW Fair Trading process]
Incidents, near-misses and stopping a job
key_points: Anyone can stop a job if it's unsafe. Nobody is ever criticised for it. If you're unsure, stop and ask.
Isolate and test water and gas before starting. No exceptions.
Suspected asbestos: stop, photograph, flag in ServiceTitan, call the Install Manager (Charlotte, interim) or the office. Never cut, drill or break it.
Compliance paperwork is part of the job, not admin afterwards. Certificates are lodged on time. [VERIFY]
Only do work your licence covers. Supervised workers have a named supervisor on every job.
signoff: Completed a SWMS/site risk check on a live job with a supervisor
Demonstrated isolation and testing procedure for water and gas
Knows the incident reporting steps

Photos, videos and job notes saved to the job

Invoicing, taking payment and customer sign-off
Tags and raising a lead or follow-up
Leaving ServiceM8 habits behind

Always check customer and equipment history before you knock.
Every price comes from the pricebook or an approved template. No hand-typed prices.

confirm: Phones or tablets, and which ServiceTitan mobile features are switched on

modules.title: The Customer Visit Standard & Handling Complaints
modules.objective: Every customer gets the same premium experience, even when something goes wrong.
modules.assessor: Lead tech in their trade (Service or Install); Charlotte (interim manager) as backup
lessons: Before you arrive: confirm the day before, call when you're on the way
Arrival: on time, in uniform, shoe covers on, drop sheets down
Tell them what's going to happen: what you'll check, roughly how long, and that you'll explain options before doing any work
Listen first: confirm what they called about in their own words
Explain before you act; no surprises on time or price
Leave it cleaner than you found it and take the rubbish away
Tenants, property managers and strata buildings: access, keys, approvals
If a customer complains on site: stay calm, don't argue or blame, no refund or discount promises, call the Install Manager (Charlotte, interim) or the office, log it
key_points: The first 30 seconds set the tone. Be on time (or call ahead), look professional, and protect their home.
Customers judge the whole company by you. Never blame dispatch, the office or another tech.

On-site complaints: stay calm and listen. Never promise a refund or discount. Call the Install Manager (Charlotte, interim) or the office and log it so the Customer Service team (Abigail, Elle, Chloe) takes over the complaint.
Tenant jobs: the property manager approves and the tenant gives access. Strata: record common property vs lot.
signoff: Observed visit scored against the visit checklist by a senior tech

good_moves: Stay calm and listen without arguing or blaming
Don't promise a refund or discount
Call the Install Manager (Charlotte, interim) or the office and log it so the complaints process takes over

confirm: How the Customer Service team logs and resolves complaints

The note structure: Why called → What I found → What I did → What I recommend
How your notes become customer reports (Preventive, Private, Real Estate, Strata, Leak Detection, Strata Quote)
Urgent findings: the 'Needs attention now' flag
Tags that drive follow-up (e.g. hot-water-8yr+, ageing-flexi-hose, PRV-monitor)
key_points: Every job gets before-and-after photos and video, with no exceptions. They protect you, prove the work and feed the reports.
Number your photos and refer to them in your notes.
Record observations, not legal opinions. Never write 'illegal' or 'non-compliant' in customer-facing notes.
Flag anything urgent so the office calls the same day.

Payment methods in the field
'I already paid', 'I'm not home' and 'invoice me later'

Asking happy customers for a Google review ($100 bonus)
key_points: Payment and sign-off are collected in ServiceTitan before you leave. No exceptions without office approval.
On installs, the Install Manager (Charlotte, interim) owns payment collection and the customer's happiness. The installer collects the balance on site; anything overdue goes to Chloe.
Planned work is 50% upfront when approved and the balance on completion. Know which applies before you arrive.
Accounts customers (property managers, strata, builders) follow their account terms.
Every genuine 5-star review earns you $100 and brings in the next customer.
Chloe makes a happy call after the job. A proper walk-through and a clear warranty explanation are what make that call go well.

paths.name: Estimating & Selling Foundations
paths.who: Service Techs (they sell on the spot). Done after Field Foundations. Sales Techs skip this; it is condensed into their x1 refresh.
paths.summary: Build an accurate estimate, use and build templates, understand hours and margin, present Essential / Standard / Premium / Elite with no pressure, and collect the 50% deposit. These are the foundations for Service Techs, who quote and sell on the spot.

modules.title: Creating an Estimate
modules.objective: Estimates that are accurate, clear and deliverable.
modules.assessor: Harriet (Sales Manager)
lessons: Understand the problem: inspect, ask questions, take photos and video
Define the scope: what's in and what's not
Estimate time and materials realistically
Build the four options (Essential, Standard, Premium, Elite) on every quote
The pre-send check: price, wording, inclusions, exclusions, warranty
key_points: Diagnose first and price last.
Every estimate states what's included and what isn't, which protects the fixed-price, no-hidden-costs promise.
Realistic hours matter because the installer's time and the business's profit depend on them.

The four options: Essential is bare bones and fixes today's problem; Standard is a solid, sensible choice; Premium fixes the root cause and is where most homes land; Elite is the best outcome, future-proofed, and is presented first.
Never quote one job when the site shows more. Standard, Premium and Elite bundle the related items you found (the same rule the Sales Techs work to). Use the five standard bundles.
signoff: Five estimates reviewed for scope, hours, wording and inclusions/exclusions by a senior tech

modules.title: Estimate Templates in ServiceTitan

modules.assessor: Harriet (Sales Manager)
lessons: Which templates exist and why they keep pricing and wording consistent
Always check for an existing template first
Building a template: standard scope wording, inclusions, exclusions, materials and estimated hours
Review and sign-off before a template goes live
key_points: Templates mean every customer gets the same price and wording for the same job.
Never build from scratch when a template exists.
New templates are for job types quoted repeatedly, and they're reviewed and signed off before going live. [CONFIRM who approves templates]
signoff: Built a draft template that passed review

modules.title: Billable Hours & Margin
modules.objective: Understand what a price is made of, and why we sell on value, not price.
modules.assessor: Harriet (Sales Manager)
lessons: We never charge by the hour, but every estimate is built on hours
The price split: labour and materials, running the business, profit
Worked example: a $1,000 job
Why a 10% discount throws away half the profit
Unestimated hours and unbilled materials
key_points: The split: ~50% labour and materials, ~30% admin and running the business, ~20% profit. On a $1,000 job that's about $200 profit.
Every unestimated hour comes straight out of the profit.
A 10% discount takes $100 off the $1,000 job, which is half the $200 profit, so we sell on value, never on price.
Never improvise a price. Use the pricebook and templates.

Techs can't discount or change a price. Only Harriet (Sales Manager) or Sadie (Office Manager) can. Never offer to 'ask the office for a better price' in front of a customer: that's a discount by another name.
signoff: Can walk through the $1,000 example and the discount maths without notes

modules.title: Presenting the Proposal
modules.objective: Present clearly, with no pressure, so the customer can decide.
modules.assessor: Harriet (Sales Manager)
lessons: Present in person where possible, with the photos to hand
Show the problem, then the fix, then each option in plain language
What they get with us: fixed upfront price, lifetime labour warranty, same-day return, no hidden costs
No pressure: if they're not ready, agree a follow-up time and log it
key_points: Problem → fix → options → the Proximity promise → let them choose.
Use their photos and video. Showing beats telling.
Never prejudge what someone can afford. Present every option at every door, Elite first.
Scope. Price. Silence. Say the price, then let the customer speak first. Never discount to fill the quiet.
If they're not ready, that's fine. Agree when you'll follow up and log it in ServiceTitan.
signoff: Supervised presentation scored by a senior tech

sim.scenario: Failing hot water unit; customer balks at the price and wants to 'think about it'. (Reuse the existing sim from sales/sa8.)

Agree a follow-up time instead of discounting

modules.title: What's Changed, Your Two Numbers & Dispatch Pro
modules.objective: Lock in the current rules, and see exactly how average ticket and close rate drive pay and the jobs you get.
modules.assessor: Harriet (Sales Manager); William as backup
lessons: Kill complacency: where experienced sellers leave money on the table (autopilot, same pitch, guessing the budget)

The rules now: the promise (fixed price, lifetime labour warranty, same-day return), four options Elite first, every line from the pricebook, 50% deposit, no free discounts. Only Harriet or Sadie can change a price
Your two numbers: average ticket × close rate. Ten jobs at $2,000 vs eleven at $2,200 is +21%, because they multiply
The $200K floor: 5 leads a day × 60% × $3,387 × 21 days = $213K. Run every lead, every full day
Dispatch Pro: it ranks you on close rate × average ticket vs the median for each job type (last 30 days and 12 months). Regular shifts only, skills on file, drive-time limits, recalls excluded
Your commitment card: today's average ticket and close rate, and the numbers you'll hit by week 8
key_points: Average ticket and close rate are the only two numbers the Sales Manager (Harriet) watches, and the two Dispatch Pro ranks you on.
Small lifts multiply: +$250 ticket and +5 points of close rate takes $213K to about $248K a month with no extra days.
Saturdays only count in Dispatch Pro if they're rostered as regular shifts.
Experienced techs can test out of the rules lessons (≥90%), but everyone fills in the commitment card live.
signoff: Baseline recorded: average ticket and close rate (last 90 days from ServiceTitan) and week 8 targets

modules.title: The Clean Handover: Sell It, Hand It Over, Get Back to Selling

lessons: Who does what: you sell. The Install Manager (Charlotte, interim) owns delivery, the customer's happiness and the balance payment. (Service Techs captain the planned jobs they sell, but Sales Techs don't.)
Why the handover is the last part of the sale: an incomplete handover is the only thing that drags you off the road and away from your next lead
The handover pack: scope (in and out), materials and specials, photos and video, access, estimated hours, customer notes and expectations
Signed approval and the 50% deposit collected by you at signing, before you leave, then booked with Kim. No deposit, no booking and no materials ordered
Setting the customer up: who'll contact them next (the Install Manager), what happens on install day, and that the balance is due on completion
Scope accuracy: your hours set the installer's pay, and under-scoping causes the scope-change calls and warranty returns that land back on you
key_points: Sales Techs only sell. After a complete handover, the job belongs to the Install Manager.
The test: could the installer do this job without ever calling you? If not, the handover isn't finished.
Commission is paid on sales paid in full, so a clean handover protects your pay as well as the installer's.
You collect the 50% deposit at signing. The Install Manager collects the balance on completion.
signoff: Five handovers accepted by Kim and the Install Manager with nothing missing and the 50% deposit collected at signing
No installer calls about missing scope on your jobs for two weeks

modules.title: One Problem, Never One Job: Bundling & Never Prejudging
modules.objective: Every quote solves the whole problem and every customer sees every option, whatever the house looks like.
modules.assessor: Harriet (Sales Manager); William as backup
draws_on: Joe Crisara / Service MVP: diagnose the person, not just the equipment
Nexstar: explore the customer's lifestyle and needs before presenting
lessons: Never prejudge: a modest house is not a modest budget, and you can't see wealth or debt from the driveway
Present every option, every time, at every door. Their choice reveals the budget, not your guess
Frame the system: an ageing system failing in stages. Patching one part moves the leak to the next weak point
The bundling rule: never quote one job. Build the tiers as bundles from what you found (photos, video, CCTV)
The five standard bundles: Hot Water, Whole-Home Water Protection, Bathroom Refresh, Drain Fix-for-Good, Landlord Compliance Pack

Build options around what they told you matters, not what we'd like to sell. Whole job or small first: high trust, go whole; low trust, earn it with one great job, never go small out of fear of the number
Pricing: every line from the pricebook, no bundle discount. Cheaper means fewer lines, never a lower price
Turning repeat bundles into ServiceTitan templates
key_points: Prejudging is the most expensive objection, because we raise it for the customer.
Every quote has at least one bundled tier, built from findings, never from a script.
No bundle discounts, ever. Every line is priced from the pricebook.
If you've quoted the same bundle twice, it should be a template (reviewed and signed off before going live).
signoff: Ten consecutive quotes with every option presented and at least one bundled tier (reviewed by Harriet, Sales Manager)
Two bundle templates built and approved

sim.scenario: A tidy older home and a quiet, careful owner. The 14-year-old unit has failed; there's no tempering valve, perished flexis and high mains pressure. They say 'just the hot water, mate'.
good_moves: Don't prejudge the budget

modules.title: Trust, Discovery & the Cost of Doing Nothing
modules.objective: Earn the right to present: read the trust shift, ask better questions, and make the consequences real.
modules.assessor: Harriet (Sales Manager); William as backup
draws_on: Joe Crisara: listen more than you talk; people buy peace of mind; find the value gap
Sandler: the up-front contract (agree what happens on this visit, including that 'no' is OK)
RAIN Group: uncover goals (aspirations) as well as problems (afflictions)
NEPQ (Jeremy Miner): curious, question-led discovery and consequence questions
lessons: The up-front agreement on arrival: what you'll do, how long, and that at the end you'll show options and they can say yes, no or not yet
Read the trust signals: forward questions ('how long will it last?', 'when can you start?'), open body language, and new problems they start telling you about
Present after the shift, not before. Presenting too early is how big jobs go cold
Discovery for big decisions: how long they'll stay, what's annoyed them, what they want the house to be like, who decides
Diagnose the person: how the problem affects the people in the house
Consequence questions and the cost of doing nothing: today's planned fix, water damage in three months, the 2am emergency at after-hours rates
key_points: Ask, then listen. Technicians who talk too much miss the details that justify the bigger option.
Customers buy peace of mind, not parts. The value gap closes when they see what the fix means for them.
Consequences, not scare tactics: describe what really happens if they leave it, calmly and honestly.
The up-front agreement makes 'not yet' a normal outcome, which takes the pressure off both sides.
signoff: Observed visit (ride-along or recorded) showing the up-front agreement and at least three discovery questions before any price

sim.scenario: Says all the right things but asks only defensive questions. You're tempted to present now.
good_moves: Hold off presenting
Ask about how the problem affects them and what they'd like
Present once they start asking forward questions

modules.title: Presenting the Big Number
modules.objective: Make doing it properly once feel like the obvious choice, then hold the silence.
modules.assessor: Harriet (Sales Manager); William as backup
draws_on: Behavioural research cited in the sessions (anchoring, loss aversion, the decoy effect)
lessons: Anchor honestly: walk through total failure first (the burst, the ceiling, the damage bill), then the full fix
Elite is the hero: the 'do it properly once' option. Present it first so the options below it are visibly compromises
Elite first, with full confidence ('the option I'd put in my own home'), then narrow to the two that fit this home. Don't read it like a menu
Let them choose up: people want to be the one who says 'I'd rather just do it properly once'
Scope. Price. Silence. Top sellers pause about two seconds after the price. The silence feels long to you, not to them
Never justify and never discount to fill the quiet. Whoever speaks next should be the customer
key_points: The first number they hear sets the scale. Lead with Elite and everything below sounds reasonable. Lead with Essential and everything above sounds like a rip-off.
Say a $30K number out loud without flinching. Practise it until it's boring.
Most techs discount before the customer has even objected. Don't.
signoff: Two proposals over $10,000 presented top-option-first, with written findings and evidence

sim.scenario: A 1960s home with galvanised pipe, three leaks this year and low pressure. A couple; one is keen, the other thinks 'just patch the leaks'.

Present Elite first, then narrow to the two that fit
State the price and hold the silence

modules.title: Finance: Seed It Three Times
modules.objective: Make finance standard on every big job, so the big number feels reachable.
modules.assessor: Harriet (Sales Manager); William as backup
draws_on: Proximity Oct 2026 sessions (industry figures in them are US data: correlation, not guarantees)
lessons: Touchpoint 1, during the inspection before any price: 'Whatever we find, we've got ways to make it easy, including spreading it out if you'd ever want'
Touchpoint 2, while walking through options, tied to Elite: 'For the bigger one, some customers just pay it weekly rather than all at once'
Touchpoint 3, after the price and the silence: 'Like I mentioned, I can turn that into a weekly figure in about two minutes'
Who wants finance: cash-is-king (keeps money invested), cashflow smoothers, and the budget-constrained. Finance means savvy, not broke
Offer it to everyone with a flattering reason. Offered upfront it's a feature; offered after 'too expensive' it's a lifeline
The HomePro flow: Option → Apply → Approved → Book → Finish. HomePro sits outside ServiceTitan, so the proposal shows the full scope and real price and never mentions finance
Quoting weekly figures: always use HomePro's real numbers, never an illustration
key_points: Same line, same tone, to every customer on every big job. A throwaway line, never a pitch.
Benchmark: if fewer than 40% of big jobs are financed, it isn't being offered consistently.
Lead with the solution; finance removes the barrier. It's the 'how', not the 'what'.
signoff: Finance offered on every big job for two weeks (checked against HomePro applications)
Walks the HomePro flow from memory on a live job

sim.scenario: You've stated $14,800 for the Premium option. They go silent and look at each other.
good_moves: Hold the silence
Bring finance home as something they've already heard ('like I mentioned…')
Offer the weekly figure from HomePro, not a discount

modules.title: The Customer Who Says They Can't Afford It (and Other Hard Objections)
modules.objective: Remove the barrier, never drop the price.
modules.assessor: Harriet (Sales Manager); William as backup
draws_on: Jeb Blount (Objections): a short pause and acknowledgement, a reframe, then ask for the next step
Sandler: pain, budget, decision qualification before presenting
NEPQ: questions that let the customer state the consequences themselves
lessons: 'I can't afford it' almost never means they can't pay: they don't see the value yet, they're scared of the number, or nobody gave them a way to say yes
Separate can't from won't: 'Totally fair. Can I ask what feels like too much about it?'
Feel, felt, found: disagree without arguing
Never discount for free: if the price comes down, scope comes out. 'I can't do that price on the full job. If we do just the urgent part today, here's where we land'
'You're 30% dearer': compare scope line by line against price-led competitors
'We need to think about it' / 'talk to my partner': agree the follow-up time and what they'll decide
'Can you sharpen your pencil?' from builders and property managers
Selling is service: letting a family walk away with a dodgy patch because we were too soft to have the money conversation is not kindness
key_points: The objection turnaround: pause and acknowledge, ask one clarifying question, reframe (value, consequence or a lower tier), then ask for the next step. One at a time.
Price only comes down when scope comes out. Otherwise they learn our first number was fake.
You can't discount, and only Harriet or Sadie can change a price. Never say 'let me see what the office can do'. Step down an option instead.
A respectful 'not yet' with a booked follow-up is a win, not a loss.
signoff: Workshopped a real lost quote in deal review and re-approached the customer

sim.scenario: Door 1: you say the price and they go silent. Door 2: 'Can you do it cheaper?' on the Premium option. Door 3: 'Money's tight right now, we'll have to think about it.'
good_moves: Use the lines from the session word for word
Clarify can't vs won't
Remove scope or offer finance, never a free discount
